status_summary: Leadership aligned with the Administration replaced the prior leadership early: the International Broadcasting Advisory Board members were reported terminated in late January 2025, and Victor Morales was named acting CEO in a staff email of 2025-03-03 with Kari Lake as a special adviser. From late July 2025 Lake was styled acting CEO; on 2026-03-07 Judge Royce Lamberth (D.D.C., Widakuswara v. Lake, No. 1:25-cv-01015) held that she did not qualify under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act and could not exercise CEO powers delegated by Morales, voiding her acting-CEO actions of 2025-07-31 to 2025-11-19, and TheWrap reported that government lawyers then told the court no one was serving as acting CEO. On 2026-03-12 the White House sent the nomination of Sarah B. Rogers as CEO to the Senate and TheWrap reported that Michael Rigas, Deputy Secretary of State for Management and Resources, was named acting CEO; the Senate Foreign Relations Committee held her hearing on 2026-07-30 and no confirmation was found. The stage is implemented because acting leadership chosen by the Administration has been in place and holdover leadership was displaced, but a court held part of the acting arrangement unlawful, and a CEO nomination was sent only about 14 months into the term.

timeline.event: A report said the Office of Personnel Management had notified all members of the International Broadcasting Advisory Board in late January 2025 that they were terminated.

Axios reported that Victor Morales was named acting USAGM CEO in a staff email of 2025-03-03, with Kari Lake serving as a special adviser who could not formally lead VOA until a nominee for a related post was confirmed.

NPR reported that Lake, who had run the agency as a senior adviser and then deputy CEO, assumed the acting CEO role in late July 2025 after Morales was placed on leave, and that legal experts questioned whether she qualified under the Vacancies Act.

Judge Lamberth ruled in Widakuswara v. Lake (No. 1:25-cv-01015) that Lake did not qualify as acting CEO under the Vacancies Act and could not exercise powers delegated by Morales, voiding her acting-CEO actions from 2025-07-31 to 2025-11-19; Lake said the ruling would be appealed.
The White House sent the nomination of Sarah B. Rogers to be USAGM Chief Executive Officer to the Senate.

TheWrap reported that Michael Rigas, Deputy Secretary of State for Management and Resources, was named acting CEO, after government lawyers told the court that no one was serving as acting CEO following the ruling.
The Senate Foreign Relations Committee held a nominations hearing for Rogers as USAGM CEO.

title: Put effective acting leadership in place at USAGM while a CEO awaits confirmation
uncertainties: The ruling is known from news summaries (Bloomberg Law, Fox 9, WTOP); the opinion text was not read. Columbia Journalism Review (2026-03-20) reported that the government had appealed and sought a stay of a related Lamberth order requiring staff to be brought back, but did not say whether the appeal covers the finding that Lake served unlawfully, and the appellate status of that finding was not found. Rigas's acting role rests on TheWrap and Columbia Journalism Review reporting and was not confirmed on an agency or State Department site; whether his service meets the Vacancies Act was not examined. Whether Morales's own acting service was lawful was not addressed in the sources read. The board removal is described only as late January 2025 by a secondary report. The nomination is confirmed through the White House notice; the Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing page of 2026-07-30 lists the nominee for both CEO and Under Secretary for Public Diplomacy and notes no vote, and no committee vote or confirmation was found as of 2026-10-13. The stage is a judgment: acting leadership chosen by the administration existed for most of the period, but part of it was held unlawful and there was a reported gap with no acting CEO in March 2026.
